grammar.title: 6A: Passive (all tenses)
grammar.explanation:
We use the passive (**be** + past participle) when we do not say, know, or need to say who does the action.

If your wallet disappears, you say 'My wallet **has been stolen**' — the thief is unknown, and that is the point.

The object of the active verb becomes the new subject. 'They built the bridge' becomes 'The bridge **was built**.'

Use **by** + agent only when the doer matters. 'Gladiator **was directed** by Ridley Scott' — here we want to name the director.

Ambition **is admired** everywhere, but humility **is remembered** longer — both are present simple passive.

The passive works in every tense. 'Films **are shot** on location' (present), 'the film **was being made** when he died' (past continuous), 'the hall **will be opened** by the Queen' (future).

It is common in news and formal language. 'Many buildings **have been damaged** by the earthquake' — the result matters more than who caused it.
examples: *The bridge *was built* in 1990.* (we don't know or need to say who built it)
*Andy's bike *has been stolen*.* (the thief is unknown)
*Gladiator *was directed* by Ridley Scott.* (we want to name the director)
*The tickets *have to be collected* from the box office.* (a rule, not a person)
*Her resilience *was admired* by the whole team.* (the focus is on her quality)

practice.q: Rewrite in the passive: 'They built this bridge in 1990.'
When do we use 'by' in a passive sentence?
practice.a: Only when we want to say who did the action, like 'was directed by Ridley Scott'.

practice.q: Change to passive: 'Someone has stolen my wallet.'
